Where is Boise and how is the city laid out?

Boise is the capital of Idaho, built along the Boise River in the Treasure Valley of southwestern Idaho. The city was founded in 1863 and incorporated in 1864, and downtown sits at about 2,704 feet above sea level.

The city spreads out in several distinct areas. Wikipedia's list of Boise neighborhoods includes the North End, the Bench, Downtown, the Boise State University area, Boise Highlands, Warm Springs and the East End, Harris Ranch and Riverland East, plus Northwest, Southwest, Southeast and West Boise. Buyers will ask which part of town the house is in, so name the neighborhood first.

Wikipedia names the Boise School District and the West Ada School District as the school systems serving the area. Check the district boundary for your exact address before you describe the house to a buyer.

  • Founded 1863, incorporated 1864
  • Downtown elevation: 2,704 feet
  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 238,429 (Census Bureau)

What does Boise's economy mean for people selling a house?

Boise has a mixed economy built around technology, health care, education, government and food companies, and that mix shapes who is moving in and out of its homes. Wikipedia lists Micron Technology, Hewlett-Packard, St. Luke's Health System, Saint Alphonsus Regional Medical Center, West Ada School District, Boise State University, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, the City of Boise, J.R. Simplot, Boise Cascade, Lamb Weston and WinCo Foods among the largest employers in the area.

For sellers, a job move at one of these employers often brings a fixed moving date, and a seller who must be out by then may not be able to wait through a long listing period.

How do Boise's summers and winters affect a house?

Boise has a cool semi-arid climate, so the house has to handle hot dry summers and moderately cold winters. In a typical year the city reaches 100 degrees Fahrenheit on about nine days and 90 degrees on about 55 days. The December average is 32.1 degrees, and the temperature drops to 0 degrees or lower on roughly one night a year.

Precipitation is low, about 12 inches a year, and snowfall averages 18 inches or less. The record low is minus 28 degrees, set January 16, 1888. For a seller, that range turns attention to a short list of items:

  • Air conditioning age and condition, since cooling runs hard from June through August
  • Roof surface and attic ventilation under long dry heat
  • Exposed pipes and hose bibs on the few nights each winter that fall to zero

A cash buyer prices these items in, which is one reason a house with an old air conditioner or a worn roof can sell as-is without a repair list.

Does Boise's wildland urban interface overlay affect a sale?

It can, if the house sits in the foothills or another area the city has mapped as higher wildfire risk. The City of Boise has a Wildland Urban Interface Overlay, known as the WUI-O, meant to reduce risk to life and property in areas with higher wildfire risk.

The overlay applies to all new structures and additions built after its effective date. It also reaches renovations of existing buildings that increase gross floor area by more than 49 percent. Areas that generally include the foothills fire hazard zone use Class 1 Ignition-Resistant Construction, called IR1, while valley and desert areas use Class 2, called IR2. The city says IR1 areas will grow with annexation, generally north and west of Hill Road.

Interior renovations are not covered unless they come with exterior changes that pass the 49 percent mark. A seller with a foothills house who plans to enlarge it before listing should talk to the city planning department first, because an addition can bring the ignition-resistant rules into play. A seller who simply sells the house as it stands is not asked to rebuild it.

What disclosure does an Idaho seller owe a buyer in Boise?

Idaho requires most sellers of residential property to complete a property condition disclosure form. Section 55-2504 of the Idaho Code says anyone who intends to transfer residential real property, including non-owner-occupied rental property, must complete the applicable items on the form prescribed under section 55-2508.

Section 55-2509 then requires the buyer to sign and date a copy and return it. The Idaho Legislature lists many exemptions in section 55-2505, and several of them come up often among Boise sellers:

  • A transfer by a fiduciary during the administration of a decedent's estate, a guardianship, a conservatorship or a trust
  • A transfer from a decedent's estate, or one ordered by a probate court
  • A transfer by foreclosure sale, or by deed in lieu of foreclosure
  • A transfer to a spouse or to a lineal relative, or between co-owners
  • A transfer from a seller who has not lived in the home within the last year and who got it through inheritance or devise

If your sale fits one of those categories, the form may not be required, but a buyer can still ask about the property's condition. This page gives general information, so confirm your situation with an Idaho real estate attorney or a title company.

How do Ada County taxes and recording work when a Boise house sells?

Boise sits in Ada County, so the county assessor values the house, the county treasurer bills the tax, and the county recorder records the deed. Each year the assessor estimates what a typical buyer would pay for your property as of January 1, and the assessor usually mails assessment notices by the first Monday in June.

Property tax bills go out by the fourth Monday in November. Ada County lists December 20 as the due date for the full-year payment or the first half, with the second half due June 20. The Idaho State Tax Commission says you can appeal your assessed value to the county Board of Equalization by the fourth Monday in June, and a further appeal must be filed within 30 days with the State Board of Tax Appeals or the district court.

The Tax Commission example for a homeowner's exemption shows a reduction of $125,000 in taxable value. Idaho sets no legal limit on how much one property's tax bill can change, though each taxing district can raise the property tax part of its budget by no more than 3 percent unless voters approve more or new construction applies. Your closing agent will split the year's tax between you and the buyer, so ask for the numbers early.

What changed with Boise short-term rentals?

The City of Boise no longer requires a short-term rental license. On May 12, 2026 the City Council approved repealing the ordinance to match changes in Idaho state law, and the repeal took effect on May 18, 2026.

Existing licenses stayed valid through May 18, 2026. The city says it will keep enforcing nuisance, noise, parking, safety and occupancy rules that are consistent with state law and city code. Idaho's Senate Bill 1162 of 2025 also changed section 67-6539 of the Idaho Code so that a city or county may not adopt or enforce an ordinance that has the express or practical effect of prohibiting short-term rentals.

If you own a house that has been used as a short-term rental, the practical effect is simple: the buyer is no longer buying a city license along with the house. You should still gather booking records, platform tax filings and any homeowners association rules before you list, because buyers and lenders ask about rental history.

When does a cash sale make sense for a Boise house?

A cash sale makes sense when time, condition or paperwork would make a normal listing slow or costly. Sellers in Boise commonly look at a cash offer for these situations:

  • An inherited house that no heir wants to maintain
  • A house needing a roof, cooling or foundation work the owner cannot fund
  • A rental with a tenant in place or a vacant unit with city code issues
  • A job or health change that sets a firm moving date

Do I need a short-term rental license to sell a Boise house that was an Airbnb?

No. Boise repealed its short-term rental license requirement effective May 18, 2026. The city still enforces nuisance, noise, parking, safety and occupancy rules.

Do I have to fill out a disclosure form when selling a house in Boise?

Usually yes. Idaho Code 55-2504 requires a property condition disclosure for residential transfers, but section 55-2505 exempts several transfers, including those by a fiduciary in an estate and foreclosure sales.

Can I sell a Boise foothills house as-is?

Yes. The wildland urban interface overlay applies to new structures and to additions or renovations above 49 percent of floor area. A sale of an existing house as it stands does not trigger a rebuild, though you should confirm details with the city.

How big is Meridian and where does it sit?

The city covers about 26.8 square miles on a flat plain in the north central part of the Treasure Valley. Boise lies to the east and Nampa to the west, and the Boise River runs north of the city. The Owyhee Mountains are visible far to the south.

Because the city is so large, a Meridian house can compete with a very deep pool of listings, including many new builds. That depth is the main reason sellers with repair needs or a short timeline look at options besides a standard listing.

What is the history of Meridian?

Meridian grew from an irrigated farm community. The town was first called Hunter in 1891, then renamed Meridian after an I.O.O.F. lodge noted it sat on the Boise Meridian. The original townsite was filed in 1893.

Irrigation made farming possible, since receiving a land patent required a water source. The Nampa-Meridian and Settlers irrigation districts still serve the area, and several canals cross the city from southeast to northwest. Around 1900 settlers planted orchards and built fruit packing businesses and prune dryers along the rail line. Production continued until the mid-1940s.

  • 1900: Union Pacific spur opened, now operated by the Boise Valley Railroad.
  • 1908 to 1928: an interurban rail line connected Meridian to Boise and Nampa.
  • 1929 to 1970: the Ada County Dairymen's cooperative creamery operated, producing Challenge Butter.

That farm and canal history is still visible in lot lines and irrigation easements. When you sell, ask whether your lot has pressurized irrigation or a ditch right so you can answer a buyer's question.

Which employers and roads define Meridian?

Meridian is the home of Blue Cross of Idaho, Jacksons Food Stores and Scentsy. The Idaho State Police is headquartered in Meridian, and its academy trains all police officers in the state. The Village at Meridian, a retail and restaurant district, opened in 2013.

The street grid is easy to read. Most of the city lies north of I-84, and street names carry a north, south, east or west prefix relative to the intersection of Franklin Road and Meridian Road. From west to east the major roads are Black Cat, Ten Mile, Linder, Meridian, Locust Grove and Eagle. From north to south they are Chinden (Highway 20/26), McMillan, Ustick, Cherry or Fairview, Franklin, Overland, Victory and Amity.

Old Town Meridian centers on Main Street and Pine Street. Most industrial areas run along the railroad line between Pine and Franklin. Buyers often shop by the nearest major intersection, so use those cross streets in a listing or when describing your house to a cash buyer.

How do permits and building rules work in Meridian?

Meridian's Building Services handles permits for structural, fire, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work for residential, commercial and industrial projects. The office is at 33 E. Broadway Ave. #102, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM, phone 208-887-2211.

Services include permit application, plan review, permit issuance and field inspection. Other permits cover remodels, mobile homes, fences, sheds, garages, foundations, fireplaces and demolition. Applications, fee payment and inspection scheduling run through the online citizen portal, and a certificate of occupancy is issued after all required inspections are complete.

The City Council meets on the first through fourth Tuesdays of the month, with a work session at 4:30 p.m. and public hearings at 6:00 p.m. Planning and Zoning decisions affect nearby development, so a seller next to vacant land can check the city's hearing agendas.

  • Look up permit history before listing, especially for garages, sheds and remodels.
  • Close out open permits if you can, since an open permit can delay a closing.
  • Keep final inspection records with your other home documents.

Which school district serves Meridian?

The West Ada School District serves almost all of Meridian and is the largest district in Idaho. A portion of Meridian extends into the Kuna Joint School District 3.

That split matters when a buyer asks which schools serve your address. Confirm boundaries with the district rather than assuming them from the city name. Property tax bills also include school district levies, so the district shown on your bill is a quick way to check.

What kind of city is Nampa, Idaho?

Nampa is a Canyon County city of 120,384 residents, according to the Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025. It uses the nickname Heart of the Treasure Valley, and Interstate 84 runs through it.

The Census Bureau counts about 33.5 square miles of land inside city limits. Nampa has grown quickly. The population base in April 2020 was 100,414, so the 2025 estimate is a gain of 19.9 percent in a little over five years.

For a seller, that growth means new subdivisions at the edges of town and a mix of older houses closer to the center. The two kinds of property attract different buyers and need different kinds of repairs.

How did the railroad shape Nampa?

Nampa began in the early 1880s when the Oregon Short Line Railroad built its line from Granger, Wyoming, to Huntington, Oregon, through the site. Alexander and Hannah Duffes set up one of the first homesteads, and the Nampa Land and Improvement Company followed. Some early settlers called the town New Jerusalem because of its religious character.

Downtown's street grid runs at an angle because it follows the tracks, which run northwest to southeast. The Union Pacific line still passes through Nampa, and a history museum marks the railroad's role.

July is the hottest month, with an average daily high near 91 degrees and a record of 109. January lows average about 21 degrees, and the coldest day on record reached minus 26.

Most of Nampa is in the Nampa School District, which runs ten elementary schools, three middle schools and three high schools plus an alternative high school. The high schools are Nampa, Skyview, Columbia and Union.

Part of the city falls in the Vallivue School District, which includes Ridgevue High School in Nampa, and a few blocks lie in the West Ada district. If a buyer cares about a specific school, the district boundary matters more than the mailing address.

Two colleges anchor the city. The College of Western Idaho is a public two year college that opened in 2007 and serves about 10,000 students, and Northwest Nazarene University is a private university founded in 1913 with about 2,000 students.

Interstate 84 has four exits into Nampa, and Idaho 55 and Idaho 45 cross the city as well. Nampa Caldwell Boulevard links the city to Caldwell, and ValleyRide runs local buses. The Nampa Municipal Airport handles general aviation.

The Code Compliance and Community Relations Division handles complaints about property conditions. The city asks residents to report a vacant home that is not being maintained, by calling 208-468-5473 or filing an online complaint.

  • If you did work yourself, find out whether a permit was pulled, and tell the buyer if you do not know.
  • If you got a code notice, keep the paperwork, because a buyer will want to see it.

The town was platted in August 1883 and incorporated on January 15, 1890. The College of Idaho opened in 1891, and Canyon County was established in 1892. What shaped Idaho Falls, and what pays the bills today?

Idaho Falls grew from a river crossing into a railroad town and then into a research and service center. The settlement began as Taylor's Crossing, became known as Eagle Rock by 1866, and took the name Idaho Falls in 1891 after the rapids below the bridge.

Irrigation made the surrounding valley productive farmland. The area grew sugar beets, potatoes, peas, grains and alfalfa, and agriculture still frames the region even though the city itself leans on other employers.

Much of it, including the campus of Brigham Young University-Idaho and the Rexburg Idaho Temple, sits on top of an old shield volcano. Lava fields lie to the west and south, and the volcanic soil is the reason the surrounding country is known for potatoes.

Almost every Rexburg address is inside the Madison School District 321 boundary. Madison School District 321 serves nearly all of Rexburg. Its six elementary schools are Adams, Burton, Hibbard, Kennedy, Lincoln and South Fork.

Farming and irrigation shaped the land. Indian Creek, a small seasonal creek, runs through the city and now works as an irrigation canal filled by the New York Canal from the Boise River Diversion Dam. Because canals and ditches run through the area, a buyer's inspector may ask about irrigation rights, ditch easements and drainage on your lot.

South of town are the Kuna Caves, a lava tube, and the Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area, which holds North America's densest population of nesting raptors. The city calls itself the Gateway to the Birds of Prey, and the Birds of Prey Festival runs each year in mid-May. Kuna Days takes place the first weekend in August.

Why do so many Kuna houses come from new construction?

Kuna's growth is driven by new subdivisions replacing farms and ranches, and that shapes the resale market. The Kuna School District describes a community once made up mostly of farms, ranches and agriculture-based businesses that is now welcoming new residential developments.

The district serves the city, areas of southern Ada County and a small portion of eastern Canyon County, and it reports more than 5,700 students. It expects the student population to grow significantly over the next 10 years based on developments already approved by counties and the city.

A few rules affect what comes next:

  • Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees on developments.
  • In July 2022 the Kuna school board approved a voluntary contribution request of about $3,200 per housing unit, which developers may or may not pay.
  • School building bonds in Idaho need a 66 and two-thirds percent supermajority to pass.

For a seller, this means a steady flow of new homes competing with your listing. A resale house in a neighborhood with active builders has to stand out on price and condition.

Who approves permits and development in Kuna?

The City of Kuna handles building permits and planning through its Development Services group. The Building Department conducts plan reviews and monitors by inspection all phases of construction and modifications, and the Planning and Zoning Department is at 751 W. 4th Street, phone (208) 629-8853.

Development decisions run through two bodies. Many projects are reviewed first by the Planning and Zoning Commission, which meets the second and fourth Tuesdays of the month. The City Council meets the first and third Tuesdays and has the final say on developments in the city.

If you finished a garage conversion, deck, shed or basement without a permit, a buyer's agent or lender may ask about it. Check with the Building Department before listing so that an unpermitted item does not appear for the first time in a buyer's inspection report.

Part of Meridian lies inside the Kuna Joint School District 3, so address boundaries can matter when a buyer asks which city or school district applies.

How are property taxes billed and due in Kuna?

Ada County bills property tax for Kuna, and the main bill is due December 20 with an option to pay in two halves. If the first half is paid on time, the second half is due June 20.

Ada County uses three tax rolls, which matters in a fast-building city like Kuna:

The county explains that extra bills can arrive if you occupied a newly constructed home or made improvements. Sellers of newer Kuna houses should ask the title company whether a subsequent or missed roll bill is still open, because it can come after the primary bill.

Assessment notices go out the first Monday in June, and the last day to appeal a value is the fourth Monday in June. The Idaho State Tax Commission describes the next steps: speak with the assessor, file with the Board of Equalization, then appeal within 30 days to the State Board of Tax Appeals or district court. The homeowner's exemption covers 50% of value, up to $125,000, for an owner-occupied primary home and up to one acre, and it ends when ownership changes. For questions, the Ada County Treasurer lists taxinfo@adacounty.id.gov and 208-287-6800.

What must a Kuna seller disclose under Idaho law?

Idaho Code 55-2504 requires a person transferring one to four unit residential property to complete a property condition disclosure form. That covers sales, exchanges, installment contracts and options, and it applies to nonowner-occupied rentals too.

Section 55-2505 exempts several transfers. These include transfers by a fiduciary in administering an estate, foreclosure transfers, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, and transfers of newly built homes that were never lived in, although those sellers must still declare annexation and city service status. If you are unsure whether you qualify, ask a licensed Idaho attorney or title officer.

Because many Kuna homes are recent builds, common disclosure topics are drainage, irrigation, and the status of city services. Having those answers ready speeds up any sale route.

A median household income of $68,017 and a median age of 30.9 point to a buyer pool that includes young families. Buyers who finance may ask for repairs or credits, while a cash buyer does not need loan approval.

How does a cash sale work for a Kuna house?

In a direct cash sale the buyer does not need a lender, so the schedule depends on your readiness and on title work. You request an offer, the buyer reviews the property, and a title company handles closing and pays off any mortgage or taxes from your proceeds.

  • List what you know: occupancy, liens, back taxes, HOA status and repairs.
  • Compare the offer with listing costs, repair estimates and carrying costs such as utilities and taxes.

This route tends to fit owners facing relocation, an inherited house, a tenant problem or repairs they cannot fund. You owe nothing if you decline an offer, and a local agent can give a second opinion on a listing.

More questions about Kuna, ID

The Census Bureau estimates 31,525 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 24,011 and the 2010 census counted 15,210.

Which county collects property tax in Kuna?

Ada County does. The first half or full payment is due December 20, and the second half is due June 20 if the first half was paid on time.

Can I get an extra tax bill after selling a newer Kuna home?

It is possible. Ada County issues subsequent and missed roll bills in January and February for improvements or occupancy assessed after the primary roll, both due June 20, so ask your title company to check.

Does Kuna charge school impact fees on new homes?

No. Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees. The Kuna School District asks developers for a voluntary contribution of about $3,200 per housing unit.

Do I need a permit record to sell my Kuna house?

Not as a separate requirement, but buyers often ask about permits for additions and conversions. The City of Kuna Building Department can tell you what is on file.

Usually. Idaho Code 55-2504 requires one for one to four unit residential property, with exemptions in 55-2505 such as estate and foreclosure transfers.

Where is Moscow, Idaho, and how is the town laid out?

Moscow sits on the eastern edge of the Palouse in north central Idaho, close to the Washington line. The Census Bureau lists its land area at about 6.9 square miles, which makes it one of the more compact Idaho cities, and Main Street runs north and south through the middle of town.

The city lies in a valley below the Palouse Range, where Moscow Mountain tops out at 4,983 feet. Paradise Creek starts on that mountain, crosses town, and flows west toward Pullman, Washington. The ground around Moscow is rolling wheat country on deep loess soil, with conifer forest starting a short drive to the east.

That setting matters when you sell. Houses near the creek, on the hillsides or out toward the forest edge can look very different in condition and lot type from a 1950s house near downtown, and buyers price them differently.

How did Moscow get its start?

The first permanent settlers reached the Moscow area in 1871, and the town took the name Moscow in 1875 after earlier being called Paradise Valley. Rail lines from the Oregon Railroad and Navigation Company and the Northern Pacific had pushed the population to about 2,000 by 1890.

The territorial legislature placed the new land grant university in Moscow, and the University of Idaho was chartered in January 1889 and opened to students in October 1892. That decision still shapes the town. Downtown still has commercial buildings that date to the 1890s.

What do the Census numbers say about Moscow housing?

Moscow is a renter-heavy city. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied housing rate at 40.0 percent for 2020 to 2024, far below the 64 to 70 percent seen in Nampa, Pocatello and Post Falls.

How does the University of Idaho affect selling a house in Moscow?

The University of Idaho gives Moscow a steady base of renters and a calendar that favors certain months. The university enrolls more than 12,000 students, with over 11,000 on the Moscow campus, and its 1,585 acre campus is the largest in the state.

If you own a house that has been rented to students, expect three practical points:

  • Leases often follow the academic year, so a sale that needs vacant possession is easiest to plan around a lease end date.
  • Rental wear is common, and floors, paint and kitchens may show it. A buyer who plans to renovate cares less about that wear than a buyer who needs to move in.
  • Tenants who stay through a sale keep their lease terms, so read the lease before you promise a closing date to anyone.

New Saint Andrews College, which moved to its Main Street campus in 2003, also draws people to the downtown area. A cash buyer will look at the same questions a traditional buyer does: condition, lease status, title and the cost of any needed repairs.

What does Moscow's weather mean for a house?

Moscow has cold, snowy winters and dry summers, and the roof, the heating system and the plumbing take most of the strain. NOAA normals for the University of Idaho station show about 50.9 inches of snow in a typical year and 27.78 inches of total precipitation, with snow on the ground on about 27 days.

Winter lows can be severe. The station's record low is minus 42 degrees Fahrenheit, and the average monthly low in January is about 22 degrees. Summer swings the other way, with a record high of 109 degrees and average July highs near 84.

  • Check the roof for ice dam damage and worn flashing, especially on older houses.
  • Look at the furnace age and the insulation in the attic, since buyers ask about both.
  • Inspect exposed pipes and crawl spaces, where freeze damage tends to show up first.

A seller who cannot afford those repairs before listing can sell as-is to a cash buyer and let the buyer price them in.

Which schools, roads and transit serve Moscow?

Moscow School District 281 covers the entire city and runs Moscow High School, Moscow Middle School and several elementary schools. Two public charter schools, Palouse Prairie Charter School and Moscow Charter School, also serve families in town.

US 95 connects Moscow to Coeur d'Alene in the north and to Lewiston and the Treasure Valley to the south, and Idaho 8 runs east to Troy and west to Pullman. The Pullman Moscow Regional Airport is about four miles west, Lewiston is 34 miles south and Spokane International is roughly 90 miles north. SMART, the Sustainable Moscow Area Transit Service, runs from the Moscow Intermodal Transit Center, and the Paradise Path gives walkers and cyclists an east to west route past the university and parks.

How are property taxes billed in Latah County?

Moscow is in Latah County, and the county treasurer mails one tax bill in early November that covers the full calendar year. You can pay the whole bill or the first half by December 20, with the second half due June 20 of the following year.

Interest on a late second half is calculated back to January 1, which the treasurer describes as very costly. A postmark counts as the payment date, but the county advises hand cancellation at the post office because the Postal Service no longer guarantees a postmark on all mail.

  • The bill lists the parcel number, the legal description, the tax charges and any delinquencies.
  • A line labeled HO EXEMPT IMPRVMNT means the homeowner's exemption has been applied.
  • The tax is split among taxing districts such as the school district, the city, highway and fire districts, the library and others.

The Idaho State Tax Commission says the homeowner's exemption covers 50 percent of the value of a home and up to one acre of land, up to a legal maximum that changes over time. Details are on the Latah County tax bill page and the Tax Commission homeowner page.

What must a Moscow seller disclose under Idaho law?

Idaho requires sellers of residential property with one to four dwelling units to complete a property condition disclosure form. The requirement comes from Idaho Code section 55-2501 and the sections that follow it, and it also covers an individually owned unit in a larger structure.

The form lets the seller describe material matters about the physical condition of the property, and the statute sets mandatory statements that every form must carry. If you know about a leaking roof, a bad foundation or a failed septic system, the form is where that knowledge goes. See Idaho Code 55-2508 for the standard form.

A seller working with us still completes the disclosure honestly. The difference is that an as-is cash sale means we do not ask you to fix what the form describes.

How does a cash sale compare with listing in Moscow?

A cash sale removes the showings, the buyer's loan approval and the repair negotiation, while a listing can reach more buyers and may bring a higher price. Which one suits you depends on your timeline and the condition of the house.

  • A listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings and a lender's process.
  • A cash sale makes sense when the house needs work, the tenants are hard to move, or you need to close around a lease end or a family situation.

We make an offer based on the house as it stands. We do not promise a price before we see the property, and you owe nothing if you decline.

Can I sell my Moscow house while tenants live in it?

Yes. A sale does not end a lease, so the buyer takes the house subject to the tenants' rights. Read the lease for its end date and notice terms, and tell us about it up front so the offer reflects it.

When are Latah County property taxes due?

The first half or the full amount is due on or before December 20, and the second half is due on or before June 20. Interest on a late second half is calculated back to January 1.

Why is homeownership lower in Moscow than in other Idaho cities?

The Census Bureau reports a 40.0 percent owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024. The University of Idaho and a large student renter population are the likely reason, though the Census figure itself does not state a cause.

Does Moscow's winter affect when I should sell?

It can. The area averages about 50.9 inches of snow a year, and snow cover on the roof and yard can hide problems from a buyer. A cash offer does not depend on the season, because we inspect the house as it is.
